title: India's Consumer Watchdog Fines Zepto, PhysicsWallah, McAfee Over Dark Pattern Violations
excerpt: The CCPA's first major enforcement actions under India's dark pattern guidelines target basket sneaking, drip pricing, and confirm shaming — with 26 platforms now declaring compliance.
body:
• India's Central Consumer Protection Authority has penalized PhysicsWallah (₹5 lakh), McAfee India (₹1 lakh), and Zepto (₹7 lakh) for deploying dark pattern tactics that manipulate consumers into unintended purchases or prevent them from cancelling subscriptions.
  • The CCPA action is part of a broader compliance sweep under India's 2023 Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, which classified 13 types of deceptive design practices on digital platforms.
  • Twenty-six e-commerce and technology platforms — including Amazon, Flipkart, Swiggy, and Paytm — have submitted compliance declarations to the CCPA, while Zepto has appealed the ruling.
  • The specific violations include basket sneaking (adding products to carts without consent), drip pricing (revealing hidden charges only at checkout), and confirm shaming (using guilt-inducing language to discourage opt-outs).

Three Platforms, Three Types of Manipulation

India's consumer protection watchdog has issued penalties against three prominent platforms for deploying what are known as dark patterns — user interface designs deliberately crafted to manipulate consumers into actions they did not intend.

PhysicsWallah, the edtech platform valued at over $2.8 billion, was fined ₹5 lakh for what the CCPA described as "confirm shaming" — using guilt-inducing or emotionally manipulative language when users attempted to opt out of paid features or decline upgrades. McAfee India was fined ₹1 lakh for similar practices in its subscription renewal flows.

Zepto, the quick-commerce startup, received the heaviest fine at ₹7 lakh for basket sneaking — automatically adding items to users' shopping carts during the checkout process without their explicit consent. The company has appealed the ruling.

What Qualifies as a Dark Pattern

The penalties are the CCPA's first major enforcement actions under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, notified in November 2023. The guidelines define 13 categories of deceptive design, each targeting a specific type of manipulation:

Basket sneaking involves adding products, services, or charitable donations to a consumer's cart without their active consent. Drip pricing conceals mandatory fees — delivery charges, platform fees, taxes — until the final stages of checkout, making the displayed price misleading. Confirm shaming uses language designed to make the consumer feel guilty about opting out, such as "No thanks, I don't want to save money" as a cancellation button.

Other defined dark patterns include subscription traps (making cancellation unnecessarily difficult), forced continuity (auto-renewing subscriptions without clear notice), and interface interference (highlighting the option the platform wants the user to choose while obscuring alternatives).

"The legal requirement is not merely disclosure, but explicit and affirmative consumer consent. A pre-ticked checkbox or a product silently added to the cart does not meet that standard."

— Central Consumer Protection Authority ruling

A Compliance Sweep Is Underway

Beyond the penalties, the CCPA has conducted a broader compliance push. Twenty-six e-commerce and technology platforms have submitted declarations confirming their adherence to the dark pattern guidelines. The list includes Amazon, Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, Paytm, Google Pay, PhonePe, Nykaa, Myntra, MakeMyTrip, Booking.com, OYO, Uber India, and Ola.

The compliance declarations are self-reported, and the CCPA has indicated it will continue to monitor platforms for violations. Consumer advocacy groups have noted that the ₹7 lakh maximum fine imposed so far is negligible for companies with billions in valuation — Zepto alone was valued at $5 billion in its most recent funding round — and have called for penalties that create a meaningful deterrent.

Why This Matters for NRI Consumers

For diaspora Indians who regularly shop on Indian e-commerce platforms, send gifts home, or maintain subscriptions to Indian digital services, the dark pattern crackdown has practical relevance. Cross-border transactions often involve additional layers of drip pricing — currency conversion fees, international delivery surcharges, and platform charges that may not appear until checkout.

The global trajectory is toward stricter enforcement. The European Union's Digital Services Act already bans dark patterns. California's CPRA includes dark pattern provisions. India's framework, while still in its early enforcement phase, signals that regulators are building the institutional capacity to hold platforms accountable for manipulative design. The fines may be small today, but the precedent is being set.
